verdict: The ladder has the right shape. It is not yet sound: several rungs can pass with no evidence at all, the factory can widen its own gate, rollback is only defined for merge-train merges (a minority of what ships), and the breaker counts shipped changes per incident, so it misses loops that cross incidents and loops that never ship.

objections.claim: Missing evidence counts as passing evidence. The rungs list 'post-deploy verify + health' and 'holdouts pass (fleet)', but nothing says what happens when a subject has no probe or no deployed app. In that case the rung passes vacuously and auto-ship has no real basis.
objections.evidence: waves.md:76 says 19 of 36 vps services are unmonitored. dora.out.md:99 and :122-123 say vps, homelab, brain, dotfiles-private and every repo deployed on the mini have no deploy record, or only a floor of one. proof.md:83-86 runs holdouts 'against the deployed app' for basalt-ui, dotfiles and warden, which are a library, a symlinked config repo and the factory itself, so none has a deployed app. loops.md:87-89 has config and code_fix rungs that rely on health checks those subjects do not have. model.md:156 defaults autonomy to `auto` for every class.
objections.test: Replay the ladder evaluator against every manifest from W2. For each (project, action class) marked auto, list each evidence item the rung names that has no producer: no probe, no holdout target, no deploy event. Any non-empty row is a rung that authorises ship on nothing.
objections.proposal: Fail closed on absent evidence and do it without an owner gate. `factory manifest check` computes an effective autonomy per class. A rung whose named evidence has no producer drops to 'propose only': the PR is opened but not merged. The gap is filed as a factory Task (add the Kuma monitor, add the probe, add consumer-build holdouts). The class flips back to auto as soon as the producer exists. For libraries, the holdout is the consumers' check and build run against the candidate version, for example argo and rb built on the new basalt-ui.

objections.claim: The factory ships its own gate through that same gate. A code-fix Change to warden can alter the ladder, the breaker, the verifier, the rollback executor or the holdout runner, and it is then verified by the very code it changes. An agent Change to project.yaml can also raise its own `autonomy` level and rate limits. A bad warden deploy also takes out the component that would roll it back.
objections.evidence: model.md:12 says Project.yaml is written by 'the owner or an agent, through a Change'. model.md:156 holds the `autonomy` block in that file. model.md:210 classes warden as fleet. ADR-012:14-16 carries the ladder in the manifest's autonomy block. loops.md:89 makes rollback 'revert through the merge train', and the merge train is warden. proof.md:62 protects only the KPI scripts with a repo the loop cannot write.
objections.test: Gameday: an agent Change that sets `code_fix` rate limits to unlimited in a fleet project.yaml, plus one that makes the post-deploy verifier always return pass. Both must be refused or caught by something other than the code they modify. Separately, deploy a warden build that crashes on start and measure whether anything restores the last good warden without a human.
objections.proposal: Add an action class `factory-self` covering warden's ship path, the verifier, the holdout runner, the breaker, rollback, and any edit to `autonomy`, rate limits or holdout locations in a manifest. It is verified by the previously released factory (N-1 verifies N). It has a pinned last-known-good release that a small independent launchd watchdog restores when the factory's own canary or heartbeat fails. Autonomy and rate-limit edits may only lower limits automatically. Raising them requires the conditions to be met: probes exist and the trailing CFR for that class is within target. Enforce it in the manifest check, not by an owner.

objections.claim: Rollback is defined as 'squash merge → git revert through the merge train'. That covers only merge-train merges. Most deployments come from direct pushes and multi-commit wave pushes, and the model counts those as Changes too. Even on the train, a revert is a new Change that needs CI, the train slot and a deploy, so it is slow and can be blocked by the red CI or open incident it is meant to cure.
objections.evidence: model.md:18 defines Change as 'a PR, or a direct push'. dora.out.md:9 and :27-30 show 1418 deploys in 90 d, 451 for basalt-ui and 378 for argo, mostly Actions-on-push. Warden made 52 merges in total (baseline.out.md:178). waves.md:18-20 has waves committing directly to each repo. ADR-012:22-23 and proof.md:39 (gameday 10, 'automatic revert (squash) → redeploy'). model.md:56-58 has a Deployment `rolling_back` state but no defined mechanism.
objections.test: Pick 30 failed-deploy samples from dora.out.md:76. For each, classify whether the shipped head came via the merge train or a direct or wave push. Then run gameday 10 twice: once via a merge-train squash and once via a 3-commit direct push interleaved with an unrelated push, with CI on the default branch red. Measure time to green and the success rate of each.
objections.proposal: Make rollback a Deployment operation, not a git operation: redeploy the last Deployment that reached `verified`, by image digest, compose revision or previous launchd bundle, recorded per runtime in the manifest. Run the git revert afterwards as an ordinary Change. Require every agent-originated push, including waves, to land as one train entry (a squash, or a merge commit for the range) so the git revert is still mechanical. Gameday 10's pass criterion becomes 'previous verified version serving within N min, regardless of CI state'.

objections.claim: The breaker counts per incident within 24 h and closes after 24 h of quiet, so loops that span incidents never trip it. Four cases: a restart flap whose recurrences fall outside the 10-min reopen window and become new incidents; fix → regression → new incident → fix chains; a Renovate revert that the next run re-proposes; and a still-down service where the breaker's own pause produces the '24 h quiet' that re-arms 3 more changes.
objections.evidence: ADR-012:28-30 and loops.md:93-97 (scope 'for one incident', 'closes on a verified fix or 24 h quiet'). ADR-003:36 sets the reopen window at 10 min. loops.md:86 lets restarts run ≤ 2 per service per hour, up to 48 a day with no breaker counter. loops.md:76-77 makes a regression a new incident. baseline.out.md:177 puts the regression rate at 10.4 %. loops.md:88 says 'one per repo per run' with no do-not-reapply marker after a revert.
objections.test: Replay three synthetic histories through the breaker: a container that crashes every 40 min, a fix that regresses every 30 h, and a dependency that fails post-deploy and that Renovate re-proposes daily. Count the automatic actions over 7 days. Today's rule allows roughly 168 restarts, about 5 fixes and 7 merge/revert pairs respectively, with zero breaker openings.
objections.proposal: Key the breaker on lineage: the fingerprint set plus `regression_of` chain plus the topology subject, with a window equal to the 7 d recurrence window. Count restarts as automatic changes. A revert writes a known-bad marker (version pin or Renovate `ignoreVersions`, or bad sha in the known-error store) that the ladder checks before re-applying. The breaker closes only on a verified fix that holds for the lineage's hold window, never on quiet. Re-arming after quiet uses exponential backoff, not a full reset.

objections.claim: Loops that never ship are not counted at all. The breaker only counts automatic changes and rollbacks. Unbounded Task re-attempts with escalating engines, Witness auto-continue after API errors, re-driving stuck agents, and verification `error` retries all burn quota and spend with no counter. These land in W4, before the breaker exists in W5.
objections.evidence: model.md:46 has 'attempt failed → ready (next attempt, stronger engine)' with no cap. model.md:60 retries `error` with no bound. waves.md:95 (W4 Witness: auto-continue, re-drive). waves.md:47 schedules W4 for days 6-8 and the breaker in W5 for days 9-11. loops.md:148-155 makes quota a control input but defines no per-incident budget. D1 (report/10-open-decisions.md:6-13) caps only non-urgent spend, and incidents are 'never capped'.
objections.test: Gameday: a Task whose acceptance check can never pass, for example an assertion against a non-existent endpoint, plus a test pane that returns a transient API error forever. Measure attempts, tokens and dollars over 24 h. Pass means the breaker opens after a fixed budget and the Task moves to `blocked` with a factory Task attached.
objections.proposal: Give each Task and each incident lineage a budget (attempts, wall clock, IU dollars, Max-percent) recorded in the ledger. Witness auto-continue and re-drive are counted against it with backoff. Exhausting the budget opens the same breaker, which shows in Argo as stuck and sends no page. Ship the counter in W4 together with Witness, not in W5. Production incidents keep running past D1's non-urgent cap but still have a per-lineage budget.

objections.claim: The migration rung's rollback is 'restore / down-migration'. On a production app, restoring a backup discards every write made after it, which is irreversible data loss, one of the owner's business classes. So the rung is either unsafe as an automatic action, or every rollback becomes an owner Decision, which is a gate in disguise. A down-migration that drops a column has the same problem.
objections.evidence: loops.md:90. model.md:156 sets `migration: auto` for weatherorb, a production service with user data. ADR-014:8-9 and ADR-003:47-49 say tools that delete data irreversibly refuse to run without an owner Decision of that class. waves.md:15 counts the owner's apps and their data as must-stay-up.
objections.test: Gameday on a copy of a fleet app's database: apply a migration, write 100 rows through the app, fail post-deploy verify, and let the rung roll back. Count the rows lost, and check whether the capability limit refused the restore (owner gate) or allowed it (silent data loss).
objections.proposal: Allow only expand/contract migrations on the auto rung. The expand step must leave the schema backward compatible with the previous release, so rollback is a code-only Deployment rollback (see ver-3) and no data is touched. The contract step (drop or rename) waits until the new version has held verified for N days, and first archives the affected columns or tables to the bucket. That makes it reversible, so it needs no owner Decision. Restore stays a disaster-recovery runbook, never a rollback path.

objections.claim: There is no defined path for keeping holdouts current, so they degrade one of two ways. Every intended behaviour change by a wave breaks a holdout. If the lead or worker may update the holdout, the oracle is agent-written and agent-maintained by the same project's agents (Goodhart). If they may not, it becomes a product-direction decision (D4), which is an owner gate on every feature. On top of that, ≥ 5 scenarios per project at 30+ deploys a week, with failing story titles shown to workers, is weak isolation.
objections.evidence: proof.md:83-87 (workers see pass/fail and the failing story's title; 'no transcript contains a holdout path' is the only control). report/10-open-decisions.md:33-40 (D4: leads draft holdouts, binding after 7 days). waves.md:101 (≥ 5 per fleet project). dora.out.md:27-28 shows basalt-ui and argo at about 35 and 29 deploys a week.
objections.test: Take the last 10 done waves of argo or weatherorb and replay them against a drafted holdout set. Count how many intended changes would have failed a holdout, and for each, which actor the design lets update it. Then plant a regression that a worker could 'fix' by editing the holdout's expected output, and check that the update path refuses it.
objections.proposal: Add an explicit holdout-update path. A holdout changes only through a Change to the holdouts repo, authored by a verifier-role agent that sees the approved plan Artifact (the intent) but never the product diff, and only when the failing story links to a plan item marked as a behaviour change. The ladder records the holdout version that gated each deploy. Measure holdout churn and the rate of fail→edit-without-plan; any edit-without-plan opens the breaker. Only the initial authorship stays under D4.

objections.claim: Two problems make a confounded fix permanent. First, 'the incident's own condition resolves in its window' is confounded, because every deploy restarts the service, so a crash or OOM condition clears whether or not the change fixed anything. Second, an incident closed this way becomes a known error with a recipe that later incidents with the same fingerprint reuse automatically. With known-error matching at 0.479 and regressions at 10.4 %, this cements wrong recipes.
objections.evidence: loops.md:89 (the code_fix evidence). loops.md:72-74 (exact fingerprint means the recipe is reused within the ladder). model.md:15 and :41 (a closed incident with a recipe is a known error, closed after the 'hold'). The hold length is not specified for any class. ADR-003:21 and :51-53. baseline.out.md:177 (5 of 48 fixes regressed within 30 d).
objections.test: Over the archived ledger, take the 'fixed' incidents whose condition was health or crash type and compare the recurrence within the 7 d recurrence window between fixes that changed code and deploys that only restarted. If the rates are indistinguishable, the resolve-in-window evidence does not separate a fix from a restart.
objections.proposal: Set the post-deploy hold per condition type, derived from that fingerprint's historical inter-occurrence time: at least twice its median gap, and at least 24 h for crash, OOM or flap types. Separately, promote a recipe to 'auto-reusable' only after it has held through the 7 d recurrence window, and demote it automatically when a `regression_of` points at it. Until promotion, an exact-fingerprint match puts the recipe in the investigator's brief (the 'similar' path) instead of auto-applying it.
